items.title: The News Roundup For October 30, 2026 : 1A : NPR
items.excerpt: President Donald Trump hit the campaign trail in the final stretch of midterm season. And he’s made a number of promises to Republican voters this cycle, looking to shore up support in the communities he’s visiting. This week, in Texas, he promised to undo Biden-era methane regulations and to produce 210 million barrels of oil. The president is swinging big as seats in traditionally red states seem to be up for grabs. One high-quality poll this week, The New York Times/Siena poll. showed the race in South Carolina between appointed Republican Sen. Darline Graham, the late Lindsey Graham’s sister, tied with her Democratic opponent, Dr. Annie Andrews. The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady at its October meeting. However, two members of the Federal Open Market Committee dissented, and were in favor of raising rates by a quarter of a percent to try to bring down inflation. And, in global news, on Sunday night, 81-year old incumbent Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defied the polls — and historical precedent — by convincing more than 51 percent of Brazil’s electorate to vote for him and deliver an unprecedented fourth term. His opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, fled the country following his loss amid an ongoing corruption investigation. All the ballots from Tuesday’s Israeli election have been counted, and there’s still no clear winning coalition. On Thursday, Israel’s Central Election Committee said Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc holds 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while opposition parties have 67. And Vice President J.D. Vance reportedly sent a letter to a senior Iranian official in Tehran aimed at reviving peace talks to end the Iran war. But when Donald Trump was asked if he directed Vance to revive peace talks, he claimed the letter was about medical supplies.

items.excerpt: ## DOJ Opens Criminal Probe of California Mail-In Ballots Despite Judge’s Order Oct 30, 2026 With just days to go before historic midterm elections, the Trump administration has issued grand jury subpoenas to local election officials in California, seeking unredacted voter records as part of a criminal investigation into the state’s voter rolls. At least one of the subpoenas was delivered after a federal judge rejected the Justice Department’s effort to force California to immediately set aside 20,000 ballots from people it claims are “likely noncitizens.” Such voter fraud is exceedingly rare. The court determined the move would wreak havoc with an election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters, and discount the votes of citizens. The subpoenas order the election officials to testify before a grand jury in a criminal investigation on November 4, the day after the election. ... ## Famine Declared in Yemeni City of Taiz Amid Houthi Siege In Yemen, the governor of Taiz says the city of roughly 1 million people has entered into famine due to a weekslong siege by fighters with the Ansar Allah movement, known as the Houthis. Human Rights Watch said Thursday the siege could amount to the war crime of using starvation as a method of warfare. The famine declaration came as a Saudi airstrike on Taiz killed 13 people. That followed a Houthi attack on Aden’s airport that injured passengers and halted flights. Meanwhile, the Houthis are rejecting claims by the Saudi-led coalition that Saudi air defenses intercepted missiles fired toward Mecca.

items.title: PCE inflation report September 2026:
items.excerpt: The pace of price increases stepped up in September, keeping inflation well above the Federal Reserve's target, while the economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, according to Commerce Department reports Thursday. The personal consumption expenditures price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.5% for the month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.6%. The monthly increase was the largest since March but in line with the Dow Jones consensus, while the annual rate was 0.1 percentage point below. Excluding food and energy, the core PCE posted respective readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, in line with the consensus. While the Fed follows both measures closely, officials generally see the core reading as more indicative of longer-term inflation trends. While inflation continued to run ahead of the Fed's 2% target, the Commerce Department also reported that gross domestic product was strong in the third quarter. GDP increased at a seasonally adjusted annualized pace of 3.4%, better than the 3.1% estimate and well ahead of the 2.2% in the second quarter. Also, in September consumer spending proved resilient, climbing 0.5%, a bit below the forecast for a 0.6% gain, while personal income rose 0.2%, compared with the estimate for 0.3%. The reports come the day after the Fed voted to hold its benchmark interest rate in a range between 3.75%-4%. Despite elevated inflation readings, central bank officials insist they can afford to evaluate incoming data before deciding on their next move. ... There was some good inflation news for the period: On a quarterly basis, PCE prices rose 2.1% on the headline number and 2.5% for core, down respectively from 5% and 3.3% in the second quarter. September's price increases were driven largely by a surge in energy costs that economists fear could be spreading to other parts of the economy. Gasoline and other energy goods saw a 9.2% rise for the month while energy goods and services broadly jumped 5.4%. At the same time, services prices excluding energy and housing rose 0.4%, and housing costs increased 0.3%.

items.title: Fed’s Barkin says US central bank’s direction ’straightforward,’ the question is pace, SiriusXM reports By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Richmond Federal Reserve President Tom Barkin said on Friday that with high inflation and the economy solid, the path of US monetary policy was "straightforward," but with an open question about the pace of any future rate increases. "Inflation’s high, demand is solid, unemployment is relatively low. So I think the direction of travel is pretty straightforward," Barkin said on SiriusXM’s Business Briefing when asked if the Fed would need to raise rates again. "The question, though, is pace ... We signaled a gradual approach. Gradual makes sense when you’re not much behind the curve, where you want time to learn." At this point, however, Barkin said that businesses in his mid-Atlantic and southeastern district report both rising cost pressures and a willingness to pass those costs along, with booming investment in artificial intelligence boosting demand and an array of prices. "There are a lot of cost pressures that are hitting American businesses," from diesel fuel to computer chips or the wages for skilled labor, Barkin said. "In the context of four or five years of elevated inflation I think it is just easier to make the argument... We are going to have to" raise prices.

items.title: Trump escalates legal challenges, scrambles schedule as US midterm elections near By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON/ANCHORAGE, Oct 30 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump’s administration stepped up criminal and civil investigations into allegations that Democrats conspired to recruit a spoiler candidate in a critical Senate race in Alaska, US officials said on Friday, injecting fresh uncertainty into Tuesday’s congressional midterm election. The Justice Department’s top prosecutor in Alaska, US Attorney Michael Heyman, said at a press conference that a Wednesday New York Times article about the effort had driven a "surge" of FBI resources, adding that he had assigned several prosecutors to the case and that investigative steps were taking place "intensely and swiftly." "Every Alaskan deserves a fair election, and they’re going to get one," he said. "Anyone who tries to illegally deceive voters and interfere with the election, they’ll answer for it." Separately, the department on Friday asked a federal judge to block Alaska from certifying the election results if the Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan, loses due to the presence of a third candidate, also named Daniel Sullivan. The contest between Sullivan and Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is widely seen as one of the few Senate races that could sway control of the chamber on November 3. A record 48 million people have cast early ballots, more than any other midterm election in US history, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, with even the American-born Pope Leo casting a ballot by mail. If Democrats take one or both chambers of Congress, they intend to launch investigations into Trump’s administration and increase pressure on the president to end the war against Iran. KEY PATH FOR DEMOCRATS If Democrats cannot flip the seat, their path to a majority narrows considerably, with the party needing to win at least two other races in mostly Republican states such as Ohio, Texas, Iowa and Kansas. Trump’s fellow Republicans are likely to lose their slim majority in the US House of Representatives, according to nonpartisan analysts. The New York Times this week reported that staffers from the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Party’s Senate campaign arm helped recruit a retired teacher living in a remote fishing village who is named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr to appear on the ballot. Reuters has not been able to independently confirm the Times’ reporting. Peltola has denied knowing about any effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan, and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has also denied involvement. Sullivan, the retired teacher, has denied coordinating with Peltola’s campaign. It is not clear what, if any, laws may have been broken; both parties have engaged in "ballot stacking" by propping up lesser-known candidates to siphon votes from their opponents. Trump has called for Peltola to be prosecuted. Heyman declined to offer specifics when asked what possible crimes were being examined, saying he would let the investigation proceed. He also said the probe had been ongoing for months and that the Times report had added urgency to the investigation, but did not explain how. Peltola’s campaign has asked a judge to dismiss the Justice Department’s lawsuit, arguing it has no legal basis. CALIFORNIA PROBE The Justice Department has also pushed forward a legal case in California, issuing subpoenas to election officials as part of a criminal probe into alleged voting by noncitizens, according to copies of documents seen by Reuters. A US appeals court on Friday rejected the department’s request to temporarily block California from counting any mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters who the Trump administration alleges are likely noncitizens, the second time the court has done so this week. A lower court judge had already denied the administration’s request, finding it would potentially disenfranchise thousands of legal voters. California officials have said the Justice Department’s assertions relied on suspect data. The administration’s legal moves represent an extraordinary federal intervention in state-run elections, which are administered locally under the US Constitution. Election officials around the country have told Reuters they are bracing for further legal challenges from Washington. Trump has long sought to sow distrust of election results, falsely claiming for years that his 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden was the result of widespread fraud. Voter fraud in the US is extremely rare, studies and investigations have found.

items.excerpt: Margaret Qualley, Jack Antonoff file for divorce after 3 years of marriage NEW YORK (AP) — Actor Margaret Qualley and Grammy winner Jack Antonoff have filed for divorce after three years of marriage. Court records show the case was filed Friday in Kings County Supreme Court in New York as an uncontested matrimonial action. Qualley is listed as the plaintiff, and Antonoff as the defendant. The couple separated in July. Qualley, 32, is known for films like “The Substance” and “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” Antonoff, 42, is a 14-time Grammy-winning songwriter and producer. The couple began dating in 2021 and married in August 2023. NEW YORK (AP) — Kirk Franklin is back with his new album, "I Am What I Am," out Friday. His 14th studio project and first double album, 14 tracks are divided between contemporary music and traditional, live-recorded gospel songs. Features include gospel royalty Karen Clark Sheard and star mainstream artists like Jelly Roll, Davido and GloRilla. “This Time," featuring GloRilla, hit No. 1 on Billboard’s hot gospel songs, extending Franklin's record to ten No. 1s on the chart. Known for his crossover hits, the 20-time Grammy winner has frequently faced criticism for working with secular artists, but remains unapologetic in the name of spreading his Christian faith. ... New York (AP) — The reggaeton icon Daddy Yankee has released a new album, “La Postal,” marking another chapter in his evolving career. This 15-track concept album, which translates to “The Postcard” in English, is a love letter to various forms of adoration, including romantic, familial and self-love, focusing on themes of affection and unity. Collaborations with newer generation artists like Myke Towers, Bizarrap, and Cardi B highlight his role as a trailblazer in Latin music. The album closes with “Pokito,” a cross-cultural collaboration with Indian American superstar Diljit Dosanjh. Associated Press Music Writer Maria Sherman writes that the single is yet another example of Yankee bringing regional music to the global stage.

items.excerpt: Opening in theaters nationwide this weekend is the horror comedy Christmas at the Kringles directed by Kevin Lewis and starring Ron Livingston, Rachel Bilson, Rob Riggle, Arden Myrin, Donald Faison and Thomas Lennon. The film’s original music is composed by Émoi (Willy’s Wonderland, The Accursed, Pig Hill). No word on a soundtrack release. The movie, which follows a family starting fresh in a quiet suburb who must fight for survival when they discover their Christmas-obsessed neighbors are a brainwashing cult, forcing the father to team up with a rogue Santa on a high-stakes rescue mission, is being distributed by Briarcliff Entertainment. Opening semi-wide in several hundred theaters is the war drama The Mosquito Bowl directed by Peter Berg and starring Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgård, Ray Nicholson, Tom Francis, Dominic Bogart and Brent Comer. Explosions in the Sky (Friday Night Lights, Lone Survivor, American Primeval, Manglehorn, Prince Avalanche) have composed the film’s original music. Netflix Music has released a soundtrack album featuring the post-rock band’s score today. Check out our previous news article for the full album details and to learn more about the movie. Already playing in around 800 theaters since this past Wednesday is the horror thriller Breeder written and directed by Alex Goyotte and starring Daniel Doheny, Dot Marie Jones, Maddie Phillips and Tanaya Beatty. The film’s original music is composed by Hannah Parrott (Harlan Coben’s Shelter, The Croods: Family Tree, Head Count, U.S. Against the World, Last Three Days, When Jeff Tried to Save the World, Golden Arm). No soundtrack album has been announced yet. The movie, which follows an eccentric poodle breeder who lures a broke college student to her remote ranch with a promise of research funding, but soon learns that there’s a catch, premiered at this year’s Tribeca Film Festival and is being distributed by the Independent Film Company and Shudder. Opening in a few hundred theaters (including numerous IMAX screens) is the documentary Everest: The Other Side directed by Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi & Jimmy Chin about elite ski mountaineers Jim Morrison & Hilaree Nelson who were bound by love and the pursuit of the impossible. Caroline Ho (Mother of the Bride, La Dolce Vita, Rap Sh!t) has composed the film’s original music. Hollywood Records will release a soundtrack album featuring the composer’s score on November 13. ... items.title: Raye to Voice Character, Make Music for Benny Safdie's ‘Lizard Music’
items.excerpt: Raye has joined Benny Safdie‘s upcoming film Lizard Music. The Grammy winner will create original music for the movie, which will blend live action with CGI, according to Deadline. Star and producer Dwayne Johnson, Theo Leber, Alicia Silverstone, Tim Heidecker, Arya Parvathi, Regina Hall, Colman Domingo, Jeff Goldblum, Rachel McAdams, David Krumholtz, and Andrew Dice Clay have also signed on to the project. The film is based on the 1976 novel of the same name by Daniel Pinkwater, a wildly prolific author of children’s and young adults’ novels. Safdie wrote the film’s script based on Pinkwater’s work and Lizard Music is set to roll out in theaters on Dec. 25, 2027. Per Deadline, the film will chronicle the madcap adventures of a boy named Leber who discovers a late-night broadcast of lizards playing unearthly music. He joins up with an eccentric old man nicknamed the Chicken Man and his confidante, an octogenarian chicken named Claudia, as they nose around the universe for answers.
